new_statements.quote: a. Non-phonemic Stress 1. On 2-syllabled words. Stress is usually on last syllable but occasionally may be even on both syllables or may fluctuate between first and second syllable. (an'a:k) child 2. On 3-syllabled words. Stress is usually on third syllable. May occasionally be on second and third or rarely on first and third. (baku'lo') wild cat 3. On words of more than 3 syllables. Stress is usually on the last two syllables. (pala'ma'nA) to consider

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic and normally falls on the final syllable of the word regardless of length (disyllables: last syllable; trisyllables: third syllable; longer words: the last two syllables carry stress, i.e. final plus penult). Stress may be level across syllables or fluctuate, so the final-stress rule is a strong tendency, not exceptionless.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; for words of more than three syllables Cubit says stress is 'usually on the last two syllables', which implies a penultimate stress beside the final one (example pala'ma'nA 'to consider' marks both).
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables 'occasionally may be even on both syllables or may fluctuate between first and second syllable'; trisyllables occasionally stressed on second+third, rarely first+third. The companion sketch Clayre & Cubit (Sarawak Museum Journal XXII.43, reprinted ibid. p. 477) gives a different picture: 'Initial syllable containing vowel e is always unstressed. Two syllable words usually have even stress, final syllable being stressed only for emphasis. Three or four syllable words have stress evenly on the penultimate and final.' For the related Uma Juman (Rejang) Kayan, Blust 1977: 76 gives final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress within the phrase; Blust 2013: 186 states the same citation-final / phrase-penult pattern for many Sarawak languages generally.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited/citation forms of the Uma Pu dialect at Long Atip (Apoh-Tutoh branch, Baram basin), fieldwork Aug 1952-Mar 1953; Cubit does not distinguish citation vs. phrasal stress, so the citation-form bias Blust notes for Sarawak languages may apply. Phonemic 'emphasis' (lengthened continuants, fortis stops) is treated separately from stress (p. 467 b).
new_statements.identity_note: Cubit's study describes the Uma Pu dialect at Long Atip (Apoh/Tutoh branch of the Baram basin, Sarawak), which Glottolog equates with Baram Kayan [kys] bara1370 ('Uma Pu Kayan = Kayan-Baram'); Cubit's Appendix I adds that Uma Pu, Uma Peliau and Uma Leken show 'no significant difference'. The other opened primary description, Blust 1977, treats Uma Juman of the Balui/Rejang basin (Belaga), which is Rejang Kayan [ree] = reja1241, a sister language, not bara1370; its citation-final / phrase-penult rule is reported here only as a comparative note.

sources.note: p. 467, 'C. Additional non-segmental phonetic phenomena, a. Non-phonemic, Stress': 2-syllable words usually stressed on the last syllable, occasionally even on both or fluctuating; 3-syllable words usually on the third syllable, occasionally second+third, rarely first+third; words of >3 syllables usually on the last two syllables. Data: Uma Pu dialect at Long Atip (Baram), Aug 1952-Mar 1953 (p. 461). Page images checked visually.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages. Revised edition. Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 008. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: p. 186 (general, no Kayan-specific statement): 'Unlike the Philippines, stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo. However, unlike much of the AN world, where stress falls predictably on the penult, many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context.'

sources.note: Different Kayan variety (Uma Juman, Balui/Rejang basin = Rejang Kayan [ree], reja1241), not Baram Kayan. p. 33: 'Stress, which falls on the final syllable of citation forms but on the penultimate syllable of forms in context in most of the languages described'; p. 76, rule 8 (stress placement): 'In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase.' e.g. /tiŋaŋ/ -> [ti'ŋaŋ] 'hornbill', /mata?+ndo/ -> ['matando:] 'sun'. Affixes 'are not normally stressed' (pp. 24-25); clitic /ha?/ never stressed (p. 90s).

sources.citation: Clayre, B. & L. Cubit. An outline of Kayan grammar. Sarawak Museum Journal XXII no. 43 [1974] -- as reprinted in Southwell 1990, Kayan-English Dictionary, Appendix pp. 477ff.
sources.note: p. 477, Section 1 Pronunciation, 'Stress:' -- '1. Initial syllable containing vowel e is always unstressed. 2. Two syllable words usually have even stress, final syllable being stressed only for emphasis. 3. Three or four syllable words have stress evenly on the penultimate and final.' Partly at odds with Cubit's 1964 statement (final stress usual on disyllables).
